{
  "research_question": "How does mouse navigation performance differ across five stimulation paradigms (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, and Sham) when measured by Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, and Angular Dispersion (AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "descriptive_findings": [
    "Sham condition shows the poorest performance across all metrics: lowest Success rate (0.273), highest Time-to-Target (4.682 s), lowest Path Efficiency (0.308), lowest Average Speed (10.737 units/s), and lowest AD (0.236), suggesting passive navigation without stimulation yields substantially degraded performance.",
    "Combined stimulation yields the best or near-best performance on most metrics: high Success (0.780), fast Time-to-Target (2.562 s), good Path Efficiency (0.502), highest Average Speed (12.833 units/s), and highest AD (0.399), indicating that multimodal stimulation (ICMS + visual) produces superior navigation.",
    "Bright Visual Only performs similarly to Combined on Success (0.785 vs 0.780) and Time-to-Target (2.614 vs 2.562), with comparable Path Efficiency (0.504), suggesting bright visual cues alone may be nearly as effective as combined stimulation.",
    "Dim Visual Only and ICMS Only show intermediate performance, with Success rates around 0.67-0.69, slower Time-to-Target (~3.0-3.1 s), and lower Path Efficiency (~0.43-0.43) compared to Combined and Bright Visual Only, indicating that unimodal stimulation provides benefit over Sham but falls short of multimodal or bright visual conditions.",
    "AD follows a gradient from Sham (0.236) < Dim Visual Only (0.336) < ICMS Only (0.354) < Bright Visual Only (0.387) < Combined (0.399), with higher values associated with better performance outcomes, suggesting angular dispersion may reflect more active or directed movement strategies.",
    "The rank ordering of conditions by Success and efficiency metrics generally follows: Combined ≈ Bright Visual Only > Dim Visual Only ≈ ICMS Only >> Sham."
  ],
  "strongest_group_differences": [
    "Sham versus all active stimulation conditions shows the largest effect: Success rates are 2.5-2.9× higher with stimulation, Time-to-Target is reduced by 38-45%, and Path Efficiency increases by 40-63% compared to Sham.",
    "The Success rate gap between Sham (0.273) and the best-performing conditions (Combined: 0.780, Bright Visual Only: 0.785) represents an absolute difference of ~51 percentage points, the largest observed pairwise difference.",
    "Time-to-Target shows substantial separation: Sham (4.682 s) is 1.5× longer than ICMS Only/Dim Visual Only (~3.0-3.1 s) and 1.8× longer than Combined/Bright Visual Only (~2.6 s).",
    "Average Speed is lowest in Sham (10.737) versus highest in Combined (12.833), a 19.6% difference, though this is more compressed than other metrics.",
    "Path Efficiency in Sham (0.308) is 38% lower than Dim Visual Only/ICMS Only (0.43) and 54% lower than Combined/Bright Visual Only (0.50), indicating substantially more tortuous paths without stimulation.",
    "AD shows the most pronounced relative difference: Sham (0.236) is 41% lower than ICMS Only (0.354) and 69% lower than Combined (0.399), suggesting markedly straighter or more constrained movement patterns in the absence of stimulation."
  ],
  "practical_interpretation": "The data support that any form of sensory stimulation substantially improves mouse navigation performance compared to no stimulation (Sham). Combined ICMS and visual stimulation produces optimal performance, but critically, bright visual stimulation alone achieves nearly equivalent outcomes—suggesting that visual cues may be the primary driver of navigation improvement in this task. Dim visual cues and ICMS alone provide intermediate benefits, indicating partial redundancy but also potential complementarity between modalities. The angular dispersion measure (AD) appears to index movement quality, with higher values associated with faster, more direct, and more successful trajectories. These findings imply that sensory augmentation—particularly strong visual feedback—can effectively substitute for or enhance intrinsic navigational capabilities in this mouse model.",
  "limitations": [
    "These are descriptive group means without statistical inference; no p-values, confidence intervals, or effect sizes are provided to quantify uncertainty or significance of between-group differences.",
    "No information on within-mouse variability or repeated-measures structure is available, preventing assessment of whether differences persist after accounting for individual mouse effects (n=8 mice total).",
    "The Combined condition dominates the sample (63.7% of trials, n=48846) versus Sham (4.6%, n=3505), creating substantial imbalance that may affect the stability and comparability of group estimates.",
    "Success is binary but treated as a mean; no information on trial-level structure or temporal dynamics (learning effects, fatigue) is available.",
    "The AD variable lacks explicit definition of its measurement scale or directional interpretation in the source documentation, though context suggests higher values indicate more dispersed/directed angular movement.",
    "No covariates (e.g., trial number, target distance/difficulty, time of day) are controlled for in these marginal summaries.",
    "Causal claims about stimulation efficacy are speculative without randomization details or experimental design information beyond the provided artifacts."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Conduct a mixed-effects regression analysis with Mouse as a random intercept, Stim Paradigm as a fixed effect, and appropriate response variable distributions (logistic for Success, possibly log-normal or gamma for Time-to-Target and Speed, beta for Path Efficiency and AD bounded at 1), including post-hoc pairwise comparisons with multiplicity adjustment to identify which stimulation conditions significantly differ. Additionally, examine trial-level trajectories and learning curves within mice to assess whether paradigm effects are consistent across sessions, and consider propensity-weighted or resampling approaches to address the severe sample imbalance between Combined and Sham conditions."
}
